title: Epidemiology
source_note: Grounded in standard epidemiology curriculum: disease frequency and association measures, study designs, outbreak investigation, screening test evaluation, bias/confounding, causation, and the natural history/chain of infection, as taught in NUC-aligned microbiology programmes. Kept distinct from MCB306 (Public Health Microbiology) by focusing on epidemiologic methods and quantitative disease-pattern analysis rather than specific microbial disease agents and control measures.

questions.question: What is 'epidemiology' most accurately defined as?
options: The study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, and the application of this study to control health problems
The study of the structure and classification of microorganisms
The clinical treatment of individual patients with infectious disease
The manufacture of vaccines and antimicrobial drugs
questions.correct_answer: The study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, and the application of this study to control health problems
questions.explanation: Epidemiology is a population-level discipline concerned with patterns (distribution) and causes (determinants) of disease, distinct from clinical medicine which focuses on individual patients.

questions.question: What is 'incidence' in epidemiology?
options: The number of new cases of a disease occurring in a defined population during a specified period of time
The total number of existing cases (new and old) of a disease in a population at a given point in time
The number of deaths caused by a disease in a population
The proportion of a population that has ever been exposed to a risk factor
questions.correct_answer: The number of new cases of a disease occurring in a defined population during a specified period of time
questions.explanation: Incidence measures the rate at which new cases arise over a period, making it a key indicator of the risk of developing a disease, as distinct from prevalence which counts all existing cases.

questions.question: What is 'prevalence' in epidemiology?
options: The proportion of a population that has a particular disease (new and pre-existing cases) at a specific point in time or over a specified period
The number of new cases of a disease arising over a year
The rate at which a disease causes death among infected persons
The number of people vaccinated against a disease
questions.correct_answer: The proportion of a population that has a particular disease (new and pre-existing cases) at a specific point in time or over a specified period
questions.explanation: Prevalence is a snapshot measure of existing disease burden in a population, combining both newly diagnosed and previously diagnosed ongoing cases.

questions.question: For a chronic disease with a long average duration, how would prevalence typically compare with incidence, all else being equal?
options: Prevalence would tend to be higher than incidence, because cases accumulate and persist in the population over time
Prevalence would always be lower than incidence, regardless of disease duration
Prevalence and incidence are always numerically identical
Prevalence cannot be calculated for chronic diseases
questions.correct_answer: Prevalence would tend to be higher than incidence, because cases accumulate and persist in the population over time
questions.explanation: Because prevalence accumulates existing cases while a disease persists, long disease duration causes prevalence to exceed the incidence rate, following the approximate relationship prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration.

questions.question: In a cohort study comparing an exposed group to an unexposed group, 'relative risk' (risk ratio) is calculated as which of the following?
options: The incidence of disease in the exposed group divided by the incidence of disease in the unexposed group
The odds of exposure among cases divided by the odds of exposure among controls
The total number of cases in the study divided by the total population studied
The difference between the incidence in the exposed and unexposed groups
questions.correct_answer: The incidence of disease in the exposed group divided by the incidence of disease in the unexposed group
questions.explanation: Relative risk directly compares the incidence (risk) of disease between an exposed and an unexposed group, and can only be calculated when incidence data from a cohort or trial design is available.

questions.question: A relative risk of 3.0 for lung cancer among smokers compared to non-smokers means which of the following?
options: Smokers are three times as likely to develop lung cancer as non-smokers
Three percent of smokers will develop lung cancer
Smoking causes exactly 3 additional cases of lung cancer per year
Non-smokers are three times as likely to develop lung cancer as smokers
questions.correct_answer: Smokers are three times as likely to develop lung cancer as non-smokers
questions.explanation: A relative risk (risk ratio) of 3.0 indicates the risk of disease in the exposed group is three times that in the unexposed group.

questions.question: In a case-control study, why is the 'odds ratio' used as the measure of association instead of relative risk?
options: Because case-control studies select participants based on disease status, so true incidence in the population cannot be directly calculated, making relative risk inappropriate
Because odds ratios are always easier to calculate by hand than relative risk
Because case-control studies never involve any exposed individuals
Because odds ratio and relative risk always give identical numerical results in every study design
questions.correct_answer: Because case-control studies select participants based on disease status, so true incidence in the population cannot be directly calculated, making relative risk inappropriate
questions.explanation: Since case-control studies start by selecting cases and controls rather than following exposed and unexposed cohorts over time, incidence cannot be measured directly, so the odds ratio is used as an approximation of relative risk.

questions.question: What does an odds ratio (or relative risk) equal to 1.0 indicate about the association between an exposure and a disease?
options: There is no association between the exposure and the disease
The exposure completely prevents the disease
The exposure doubles the risk of disease
The study must have been conducted incorrectly
questions.correct_answer: There is no association between the exposure and the disease
questions.explanation: A value of 1.0 means the risk (or odds) of disease is the same in the exposed and unexposed groups, indicating no association, as opposed to values above or below 1 which suggest increased or decreased risk respectively.

questions.question: What is 'attributable risk' (risk difference)?
options: The absolute difference in incidence of disease between the exposed and unexposed groups, representing the excess risk due to the exposure
The ratio of incidence in the exposed group to incidence in the unexposed group
The total number of cases attributable to any cause whatsoever in a population
The proportion of controls who were exposed to a risk factor
questions.correct_answer: The absolute difference in incidence of disease between the exposed and unexposed groups, representing the excess risk due to the exposure
questions.explanation: Attributable risk quantifies the actual excess incidence of disease that can be attributed to the exposure, useful for assessing public health impact, unlike relative risk which is a ratio.

questions.question: In a 'cohort study', participants are enrolled and classified based on what?
options: Their exposure status, and then followed forward over time to observe who develops the disease of interest
Their disease status, and their past exposure history is then investigated retrospectively
Random assignment to receive a specific intervention, controlled by the investigator
Their geographic location alone, with no consideration of exposure or disease status
questions.correct_answer: Their exposure status, and then followed forward over time to observe who develops the disease of interest
questions.explanation: A cohort study is fundamentally a follow-up (often prospective) design comparing disease occurrence between groups defined by exposure status at the start of the study.

questions.question: In a 'case-control study', participants are enrolled and classified based on what?
options: Their disease status (cases with the disease vs. controls without it), and their past exposure history is investigated retrospectively
Their exposure status, then followed forward to see who develops disease
Random allocation to treatment or placebo groups
The severity of their symptoms only, with exposure never assessed
questions.correct_answer: Their disease status (cases with the disease vs. controls without it), and their past exposure history is investigated retrospectively
questions.explanation: Case-control studies work backward from outcome to exposure, comparing the exposure history of individuals with the disease (cases) to those without it (controls).

questions.question: Which epidemiological study design is generally considered to provide the strongest evidence for a causal relationship, due to random allocation of exposure/intervention?
options: Randomised controlled trial (RCT)
Case report
Ecological study
Cross-sectional study
questions.correct_answer: Randomised controlled trial (RCT)
questions.explanation: Because random allocation balances both known and unknown confounding factors between groups, the RCT design offers the strongest study-design-based evidence for causation among observational and experimental designs.

questions.question: What is a key limitation of a 'cross-sectional study' when investigating disease causation?
options: Because exposure and disease status are measured at the same point in time, it is often difficult to establish which occurred first (temporal sequence)
It can never include information about disease prevalence
It always requires many years of follow-up, making it very expensive
It cannot be used to study any chronic disease
questions.correct_answer: Because exposure and disease status are measured at the same point in time, it is often difficult to establish which occurred first (temporal sequence)
questions.explanation: Cross-sectional studies capture a single snapshot, so the simultaneous measurement of exposure and outcome makes it hard to determine temporal (cause-before-effect) sequence, a key requirement for causal inference.

questions.question: What is an 'ecological study' in epidemiology?
options: A study that examines the relationship between exposure and disease using aggregate (group-level) data for entire populations, rather than individual-level data
A study conducted exclusively in forests or natural habitats
A study that follows a single individual over their entire lifetime
A randomised trial comparing two competing drug treatments
questions.correct_answer: A study that examines the relationship between exposure and disease using aggregate (group-level) data for entire populations, rather than individual-level data
questions.explanation: Ecological studies analyse correlations using population-level (aggregate) exposure and outcome data, which can be useful for generating hypotheses but is prone to the ecological fallacy.

questions.question: What is the 'ecological fallacy'?
options: The error of assuming that an association observed at the group/population level necessarily applies to individuals within that group
The mistaken belief that ecosystems have no effect on disease transmission
A bias that only occurs in randomised controlled trials
The failure to adjust for confounding in a cohort study
questions.correct_answer: The error of assuming that an association observed at the group/population level necessarily applies to individuals within that group
questions.explanation: The ecological fallacy is the specific error of drawing conclusions about individual-level relationships purely from group-level (aggregate) data.

questions.question: The three main variables examined in descriptive epidemiology are commonly summarised as which of the following?
options: Person, place, and time
Agent, host, and environment
Sensitivity, specificity, and predictive value
Incidence, prevalence, and mortality
questions.correct_answer: Person, place, and time
questions.explanation: Descriptive epidemiology characterises the occurrence of disease according to who is affected (person), where (place), and when (time), forming the basis for generating hypotheses about causation.

questions.question: What is the 'epidemiologic triad' (or triangle) traditionally used to describe the causation of infectious disease?
options: Agent, host, and environment
Incidence, prevalence, and duration
Exposure, outcome, and confounder
Sensitivity, specificity, and prevalence
questions.correct_answer: Agent, host, and environment
questions.explanation: The epidemiologic triad conceptualises disease as arising from an interaction between a causative agent, a susceptible host, and the surrounding environment that brings them together.

questions.question: What is meant by the 'chain of infection'?
options: The sequence of linked elements — infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and susceptible host — that must all be present for an infectious disease to spread
The order in which vaccines must be administered to a patient
The list of hospital departments a patient passes through during treatment
The sequence of steps followed in conducting a systematic literature review
questions.correct_answer: The sequence of linked elements — infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and susceptible host — that must all be present for an infectious disease to spread
questions.explanation: The chain of infection model identifies the linked components required for transmission, and breaking any single link can prevent or control the spread of disease.

questions.question: What is a 'reservoir' of infection in epidemiology?
options: A living organism or inanimate environment in which an infectious agent normally lives, grows, and multiplies, and on which it depends for survival
The specific syringe used to administer a vaccine
A laboratory device used to culture bacteria
A synonym for 'vector', meaning any insect that transmits disease
questions.correct_answer: A living organism or inanimate environment in which an infectious agent normally lives, grows, and multiplies, and on which it depends for survival
questions.explanation: A reservoir (which may be human, animal, or environmental) is the natural habitat where the infectious agent survives, potentially serving as a continuing source of infection.

questions.question: What is a disease 'vector'?
options: A living organism, typically an arthropod such as a mosquito, that transmits an infectious agent from one host to another
The chemical structure of a pathogen's cell wall
A synonym for the causative agent itself
A measure of how contagious a disease is
questions.correct_answer: A living organism, typically an arthropod such as a mosquito, that transmits an infectious agent from one host to another
questions.explanation: Vectors, such as mosquitoes transmitting malaria or ticks transmitting Lyme disease, actively carry and transmit pathogens between hosts, distinguishing vector-borne transmission from direct or fomite transmission.

questions.question: What is 'herd immunity'?
options: Indirect protection from an infectious disease that occurs when a sufficiently large proportion of a population is immune, reducing the likelihood of transmission to susceptible individuals
The immunity an individual develops after their first infection, regardless of population-level immunity
A vaccine given exclusively to livestock
The total number of people vaccinated in a country
questions.correct_answer: Indirect protection from an infectious disease that occurs when a sufficiently large proportion of a population is immune, reducing the likelihood of transmission to susceptible individuals
questions.explanation: Herd immunity reduces disease spread by lowering the probability that an infected individual will contact a susceptible one, indirectly protecting even those who are not themselves immune.

questions.question: What does the 'basic reproduction number' (R0) represent?
options: The average number of secondary infections produced by a single infectious individual in a completely susceptible population
The total number of people who have ever been infected by a disease worldwide
The percentage of a population that must be vaccinated to eliminate a disease
The case fatality rate of a disease
questions.correct_answer: The average number of secondary infections produced by a single infectious individual in a completely susceptible population
questions.explanation: R0 indicates the transmission potential of an infectious agent in a fully susceptible population; if R0 is greater than 1, the disease can spread, and if less than 1, it will tend to die out.

questions.question: If a disease has an R0 greater than 1 with no intervention, what does this imply about its potential to spread in a susceptible population?
options: The number of cases is expected to increase over time, as each infected person on average infects more than one other person
The disease will automatically die out within one generation
The disease can never become an epidemic
Every person in the population will definitely become infected within a week
questions.correct_answer: The number of cases is expected to increase over time, as each infected person on average infects more than one other person
questions.explanation: An R0 greater than 1 means, on average, transmission is self-sustaining and increasing, which is the condition required for an outbreak to grow into an epidemic in the absence of control measures.

questions.question: What is the first key step typically undertaken when investigating a suspected disease outbreak?
options: Verifying the diagnosis and confirming that a true outbreak exists (i.e., that case numbers genuinely exceed the expected baseline)
Immediately closing all public facilities in the affected area
Publishing the final investigation report to the media
Vaccinating the entire national population regardless of the disease involved
questions.correct_answer: Verifying the diagnosis and confirming that a true outbreak exists (i.e., that case numbers genuinely exceed the expected baseline)
questions.explanation: Before extensive investigation, the outbreak investigator must confirm the diagnosis is accurate and that observed cases genuinely exceed the expected number for that place and time, ruling out reporting artefacts.

questions.question: In outbreak investigation, what is a 'case definition' used for?
options: A standardised set of criteria used to decide whether a person should be classified as having the disease or condition under investigation
The legal definition of a crime committed by an infected individual
A list of every hospital in the affected geographic area
The dosage instructions for a treatment drug
questions.correct_answer: A standardised set of criteria used to decide whether a person should be classified as having the disease or condition under investigation
questions.explanation: A consistent case definition, typically combining clinical, laboratory, and time/place/person criteria, ensures cases are identified and counted uniformly throughout an investigation.

questions.question: What is an 'epidemic curve' (epi curve) used to display in an outbreak investigation?
options: The distribution of cases of a disease over time (by date of onset), helping to identify the pattern and likely mode of transmission of the outbreak
The geographic distribution of cases on a map
The age distribution of the general population
The cost of treating each case of disease
questions.correct_answer: The distribution of cases of a disease over time (by date of onset), helping to identify the pattern and likely mode of transmission of the outbreak
questions.explanation: An epidemic curve is a histogram of case counts by time of onset, and its shape (e.g. a sharp single peak vs. a prolonged pattern) helps investigators infer whether the outbreak had a common source or was propagated person-to-person.

questions.question: A single, sharp peak on an epidemic curve, with all cases occurring within roughly one incubation period, is most characteristic of which type of outbreak?
options: A common-source, point-source outbreak, such as contamination of a single shared food item at one event
A propagated (person-to-person) outbreak occurring over several successive waves
A slowly, continuously emerging chronic disease with no discrete source
An outbreak with no identifiable source at all
questions.correct_answer: A common-source, point-source outbreak, such as contamination of a single shared food item at one event
questions.explanation: A point-source outbreak, where everyone is exposed to the same source at roughly the same time, typically produces a single sharp peak on the epi curve corresponding to the common incubation period.

questions.question: What is the difference between an 'endemic', 'epidemic', and 'pandemic' disease pattern?
options: Endemic is the constant, expected baseline presence of a disease in a population; epidemic is a sudden increase above that expected baseline; pandemic is an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents
Endemic means a disease has been completely eradicated worldwide
Epidemic and pandemic are two names for exactly the same scale of disease occurrence
Endemic refers only to diseases affecting animals, never humans
questions.correct_answer: Endemic is the constant, expected baseline presence of a disease in a population; epidemic is a sudden increase above that expected baseline; pandemic is an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents
questions.explanation: These three terms represent an escalating scale of disease spread: endemic (steady baseline), epidemic (unusual increase in a defined area), and pandemic (widespread international/global epidemic).

questions.question: What is 'surveillance' in public health epidemiology?
options: The ongoing, systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of health data essential for planning, implementing, and evaluating public health action
The covert monitoring of individual citizens by security agencies
A one-time survey conducted only after an outbreak has ended
The process of manufacturing diagnostic test kits
questions.correct_answer: The ongoing, systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of health data essential for planning, implementing, and evaluating public health action
questions.explanation: Public health surveillance is a continuous process enabling early detection of health trends and outbreaks, and timely dissemination of information to those who need it for action.

questions.question: In evaluating a diagnostic/screening test, 'sensitivity' refers to which of the following?
options: The proportion of people who truly have the disease who are correctly identified as positive by the test
The proportion of people who truly do not have the disease who are correctly identified as negative by the test
The proportion of positive test results that are truly positive
The proportion of negative test results that are truly negative
questions.correct_answer: The proportion of people who truly have the disease who are correctly identified as positive by the test
questions.explanation: Sensitivity measures a test's ability to correctly detect disease among those who genuinely have it (true positive rate), which is critical for screening tests aiming to minimise missed cases.

questions.question: In evaluating a diagnostic/screening test, 'specificity' refers to which of the following?
options: The proportion of people who truly do not have the disease who are correctly identified as negative by the test
The proportion of people who truly have the disease who are correctly identified as positive by the test
The overall accuracy of the test regardless of disease status
The cost of administering the test to the population
questions.correct_answer: The proportion of people who truly do not have the disease who are correctly identified as negative by the test
questions.explanation: Specificity measures a test's ability to correctly rule out disease in people who do not have it (true negative rate), important for minimising false alarms.

questions.question: What is 'positive predictive value' (PPV) of a diagnostic test?
options: The proportion of people with a positive test result who actually have the disease
The proportion of people with the disease who test positive
The proportion of people without the disease who test negative
The overall prevalence of the disease in the tested population
questions.correct_answer: The proportion of people with a positive test result who actually have the disease
questions.explanation: PPV answers the clinically relevant question 'given a positive result, how likely is this person to truly have the disease?' and, unlike sensitivity/specificity, is heavily influenced by disease prevalence in the tested population.

questions.question: How does the prevalence of a disease in the population being tested affect the positive predictive value (PPV) of a screening test, holding sensitivity and specificity constant?
options: As prevalence decreases, PPV tends to decrease, because a larger proportion of positive results become false positives
PPV is completely independent of disease prevalence
As prevalence decreases, PPV always increases
Prevalence only affects sensitivity, never PPV
questions.correct_answer: As prevalence decreases, PPV tends to decrease, because a larger proportion of positive results become false positives
questions.explanation: In a low-prevalence population, even a specific test generates a high number of false positives relative to true positives, reducing PPV — a key reason screening in low-risk populations can yield many false-positive results.

questions.question: What is 'confounding' in an epidemiological study?
options: A distortion of the observed association between an exposure and an outcome caused by a third factor that is independently related to both the exposure and the outcome
A type of measurement error caused by a faulty laboratory instrument
The deliberate falsification of study data by a researcher
The natural variation in disease incidence from one year to the next
questions.correct_answer: A distortion of the observed association between an exposure and an outcome caused by a third factor that is independently related to both the exposure and the outcome
questions.explanation: A confounding variable is associated with both the exposure and the outcome (without being on the causal pathway between them), and can create a spurious or masked association if not controlled for.

questions.question: What is 'selection bias' in an epidemiological study?
options: A systematic error arising from the way study participants are selected or retained, leading to a study sample that is not representative of the population intended to be studied
An error that occurs only during statistical data analysis, never during participant recruitment
A type of bias that can be entirely eliminated by increasing the sample size alone
A bias that exclusively affects randomised controlled trials
questions.correct_answer: A systematic error arising from the way study participants are selected or retained, leading to a study sample that is not representative of the population intended to be studied
questions.explanation: Selection bias distorts study validity when the process of enrolling or retaining subjects systematically differs between comparison groups in a way related to exposure or outcome.

questions.question: What is 'recall bias', and in which study design does it most commonly pose a threat?
options: Systematic differences in the accuracy or completeness of participants' memories about past exposures, most commonly affecting retrospective case-control studies
A bias that only affects laboratory equipment calibration
A bias arising exclusively in randomised controlled trials with blinding
A bias caused only by errors in a study's statistical software
questions.correct_answer: Systematic differences in the accuracy or completeness of participants' memories about past exposures, most commonly affecting retrospective case-control studies
questions.explanation: Because case-control studies rely on participants recalling past exposures, cases (who may search harder for an explanation for their illness) can differentially over- or under-report exposure compared to controls, biasing results.

questions.question: Among the Bradford Hill criteria for assessing causation, what does 'biological gradient' (dose-response relationship) refer to?
options: The observation that increasing levels or duration of exposure are associated with a correspondingly increasing risk of the disease
The requirement that the exposure must always precede the disease in time
The strength of the statistical association between exposure and outcome
The consistency of findings across multiple different studies and populations
questions.correct_answer: The observation that increasing levels or duration of exposure are associated with a correspondingly increasing risk of the disease
questions.explanation: A dose-response (biological gradient) relationship, where greater exposure is linked to greater disease risk, strengthens the case for a causal relationship, as one of several Bradford Hill considerations.

questions.question: Which Bradford Hill criterion for causation requires that the cause must occur before the effect?
options: Temporality
Strength of association
Plausibility
Analogy
questions.correct_answer: Temporality
questions.explanation: Temporality is considered the only truly indispensable Bradford Hill criterion: the exposure must precede the onset of disease for a causal relationship to be logically possible.

questions.question: What does the 'natural history of disease' describe?
options: The progression of a disease process in an individual over time, from exposure/pre-exposure through the biological onset, and on to resolution, disability, or death, in the absence of intervention
The historical timeline of when a pathogen species first evolved
The geographic spread of a pathogen across continents over centuries
A record of which laboratory first isolated a particular pathogen
questions.correct_answer: The progression of a disease process in an individual over time, from exposure/pre-exposure through the biological onset, and on to resolution, disability, or death, in the absence of intervention
questions.explanation: Natural history describes the unmodified course a disease would take in an individual, forming the basis for identifying appropriate points at which to apply levels of prevention.

questions.question: What is the distinction between 'primary', 'secondary', and 'tertiary' prevention in the natural history of disease framework?
options: Primary prevention aims to prevent disease onset before it occurs; secondary prevention aims for early detection and treatment of existing but early-stage disease; tertiary prevention aims to reduce complications and disability from established disease
Primary prevention treats only symptoms, secondary prevents disease entirely, and tertiary is only used for terminal illness
All three levels apply exclusively to non-communicable diseases and never to infectious diseases
Primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention are simply three different names for the same intervention
questions.correct_answer: Primary prevention aims to prevent disease onset before it occurs; secondary prevention aims for early detection and treatment of existing but early-stage disease; tertiary prevention aims to reduce complications and disability from established disease
questions.explanation: This classic framework of prevention levels corresponds to distinct points along the natural history of disease: before onset, during the early/subclinical stage, and after disease is clinically established.

questions.question: A vaccination programme delivered to healthy individuals to prevent them from ever contracting a disease is an example of which level of prevention?
options: Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Tertiary prevention
Quaternary prevention
questions.correct_answer: Primary prevention
questions.explanation: Vaccination reduces the risk of disease before exposure/onset occurs, which is the defining feature of primary prevention.

questions.question: What is a 'notifiable disease'?
options: A disease that healthcare providers and laboratories are legally required to report to public health authorities when diagnosed, to support surveillance and outbreak control
A disease that has never been recorded anywhere in the world
A disease for which no treatment currently exists
A disease that only affects animals and never humans
questions.correct_answer: A disease that healthcare providers and laboratories are legally required to report to public health authorities when diagnosed, to support surveillance and outbreak control
questions.explanation: Mandatory reporting of notifiable diseases enables public health authorities to monitor trends, detect outbreaks quickly, and coordinate a timely response.

questions.question: What is the difference between the 'crude mortality rate' and the 'case fatality rate' (CFR)?
options: Crude mortality rate is the number of deaths from all causes divided by the total population, while CFR is the proportion of people diagnosed with a specific disease who die from it
Crude mortality rate applies only to infectious diseases, while CFR applies only to non-communicable diseases
The two terms are interchangeable and always yield an identical numeric value
CFR measures deaths in the entire population, while crude mortality rate measures deaths only among diagnosed cases
questions.correct_answer: Crude mortality rate is the number of deaths from all causes divided by the total population, while CFR is the proportion of people diagnosed with a specific disease who die from it
questions.explanation: Crude mortality is a population-wide, all-cause measure, while case fatality rate is disease-specific and calculated only among people who actually have that disease.
